title: Rotate List
approach_name: Make a cycle then break at new tail
notes:
Task and constraints: Rotate a singly linked list right by k positions. The list may be empty, and k can exceed the number of nodes.
Idea: Count the nodes, connect the tail to the head to form a cycle, reduce k modulo the length, then break the cycle after n-k steps from the old head.
Technique and why it applies: A right rotation moves the final k nodes to the front; a cycle makes that cut a simple pointer operation.
Invariant: Before breaking the cycle, every original node appears exactly once on the circular list.
Edge cases: Empty and one-node lists are unchanged. If k is a multiple of the length, the result is the original order.
Complexity: Time is O(n) to count and locate the cut. Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: The list is counted and the new tail is located with a constant number of pointers.
code:
from typing import Optional

class Solution:
    def rotateRight(self, head: Optional[ListNode], k: int) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        if not head or not head.next or k == 0: return head
        n=1;tail=head
        while tail.next:tail=tail.next;n+=1
        k%=n
        if k==0:return head
        tail.next=head
        steps=n-k;new_tail=head
        for _ in range(steps-1):new_tail=new_tail.next
        new_head=new_tail.next;new_tail.next=None
        return new_head

title: Unique Paths
notes:
Task and constraints: Count paths from the top-left to bottom-right of an m by n grid when each move is right or down. The answer can grow quickly but fits the problem's return type.
Idea: Use a one-dimensional DP array where dp[c] counts paths to the current row's column. Each cell combines paths from above (old dp[c]) and left (updated dp[c-1]).
Technique and why it applies: Every path to a cell must enter from exactly one of those two predecessors.
Invariant: Before updating column c, dp[c] is the count from above and dp[c-1] is the count from the left in the current row.
Edge cases: A one-row or one-column grid has exactly one path. Initialize every column to one for the first row.
Complexity: Time is O(mn). Extra space is O(n).
complexity_reason: Each grid cell updates one DP entry, and only one row is retained.

title: Unique Paths II
notes:
Task and constraints: Count right/down paths through a grid where 1 marks an obstacle and 0 marks an open cell. A path cannot enter an obstacle.
Idea: Maintain dp[c], the number of paths reaching the current cell. An obstacle resets that count to zero; otherwise add the paths from the left to the count from above.
Technique and why it applies: Each open cell receives paths only from its top and left neighbors, while an obstacle blocks every path through that position.
Invariant: After processing a cell, dp[c] equals the number of valid paths from the origin to that cell.
Edge cases: If the start is blocked, all path counts remain zero. A blocked destination also yields zero.
Complexity: Time is O(mn). Extra space is O(n).
complexity_reason: A single DP row is updated in place while scanning the grid.

title: Minimum Path Sum
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the minimum sum path through a non-negative grid from top-left to bottom-right, moving only right or down.
Idea: Use dp[c] for the minimum cost to reach the current row's cell. The new value is the cell cost plus the minimum of the path from above and the path from the left.
Technique and why it applies: Every valid path enters a cell from its top or left neighbor, so taking the cheaper predecessor is optimal.
Invariant: dp[c] stores the minimum path cost to the current cell after its value is updated.
Edge cases: The first row accumulates from the left; the first column accumulates from above. A one-cell grid returns its own value.
Complexity: Time is O(mn). Extra space is O(n).
complexity_reason: Each cell updates a single DP value in a one-row array.

title: Valid Number
notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether a string is a valid decimal number, allowing an optional sign, decimal point, and exponent with its own optional sign. The entire trimmed string must follow the grammar.
Idea: Trim outer spaces and validate against a grammar that permits digits with an optional decimal point and an optional exponent whose value contains at least one digit.
Technique and why it applies: The grammar can be expressed precisely with a regular expression, avoiding ambiguous ad hoc checks for each character.
Invariant: The method returns true only if the complete trimmed string matches the numeric grammar; partial matches are rejected.
Edge cases: Accept forms such as .9, 4., +3.14, and -90E3. Reject '.', '+.', '1e', and 'e3'.
Complexity: Time is O(n) for a fixed regex grammar. Extra space is O(n) for the trimmed representation and regex processing.
complexity_reason: The expression scans the trimmed string once under a fixed grammar.

title: Plus One
approach_name: Propagate carry from the last digit
notes:
Task and constraints: Add one to a non-negative integer represented by its decimal digits, with the most significant digit first and no leading zeroes.
Idea: Walk from the last digit toward the front. If a digit is below nine, increment it and return; otherwise set it to zero and continue carrying.
Technique and why it applies: Decimal addition changes only the trailing run of nines and possibly creates one new leading digit.
Invariant: After processing a suffix of nines, that suffix has become zeroes and the carry is still one.
Edge cases: If every digit is nine, allocate a result one element longer with a leading one.
Complexity: Time is O(n) in the worst case. Extra space is O(1) when no leading digit is needed, otherwise O(n) for the new array.
space_complexity: O(1) usual case; O(n) when a new leading digit is needed
complexity_reason: Only a suffix is touched unless every digit is nine.

title: Add Binary
notes:
Task and constraints: Add two binary strings and return their binary sum as a string. Input lengths can be up to 10,000, so converting to machine integers is unsafe.
Idea: Walk both strings from right to left, add available bits and carry, append total modulo two, and update carry by integer division by two.
Technique and why it applies: This is ordinary base-two column addition and handles arbitrarily long strings without parsing the whole number.
Invariant: The reversed output contains the correct low-order sum bits processed so far, and carry is the amount passed to the next position.
Edge cases: The strings may have different lengths. Append a final carry if present, then reverse the output.
Complexity: Time is O(max(m,n)). Extra space is O(max(m,n)) for the output buffer.
complexity_reason: Each input bit is consumed once and each output bit is appended once.

title: Text Justification
approach_name: Greedily pack words and distribute spaces
notes:
Task and constraints: Format words into lines of exactly maxWidth characters with full justification, except the final line and single-word lines, which are left-justified.
Idea: Greedily select the largest word range that fits. Distribute spaces evenly between words, giving extra spaces to leftmost gaps; for the last or single-word line, join with one space and pad right.
Technique and why it applies: The greedy packing rule determines line membership, and integer division/remainder determines balanced spacing.
Invariant: Every completed line contains the earliest unplaced words that fit and has exactly maxWidth characters.
Edge cases: A single-word line receives trailing spaces. The last line uses single spaces between words and trailing padding.
Complexity: Time is O(total input characters plus output size). Space is O(output size) for the returned lines.
complexity_reason: Each word is packed once and each output character is emitted once.

title: Sqrt(x)
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the floor of the square root of a non-negative integer x without using built-in square-root or exponent functions.
Idea: Binary-search an integer candidate between zero and x, keeping the largest candidate whose square does not exceed x.
Technique and why it applies: The predicate candidate^2 <= x is monotonic, so binary search finds its final true value.
Invariant: Every value at or below left is feasible and every value at or above right is infeasible under the half-open search convention.
Edge cases: x=0 and x=1 return themselves. Use division comparison mid <= x // mid to avoid multiplication overflow, with mid zero handled by the bounds.
Complexity: Time is O(log x). Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Binary search halves the candidate range each iteration.

title: Climbing Stairs
notes:
Task and constraints: Count ways to reach step n when each move climbs one or two steps. n is at most 45.
Idea: The ways to reach step i are the sum of ways to reach i-1 and i-2. Keep only those two previous counts while iterating upward.
Technique and why it applies: The final move is either one step from i-1 or two steps from i-2, and these choices are disjoint.
Invariant: The two variables hold the number of ways to reach the previous two stair counts.
Edge cases: n=1 returns one and n=2 returns two. Initialize the recurrence to match these base cases.
Complexity: Time is O(n). Extra space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Only two previous recurrence values are stored.
